suggestions.rationale: Mapping Expansion Batch ME-29 adds this relationship only as a bounded post-injury venous-thromboembolism association. Achilles tendon rupture with its associated immobilization and lower-leg injury is followed by deep vein thrombosis at substantial rates in prospective and observational cohorts, but the primary diagnosis alone does not establish DVT in every person or determine an individual's cause, severity, or course. Require independently documented Achilles tendon rupture and DVT, compatible laterality and chronology, objective venous imaging, and clinical review. Preserve inherited and acquired thrombophilia, malignancy, prior venous thromboembolism, age, obesity, estrogen therapy, major surgery, and other competing causes.
evidenceGaps: Independent documentation of the Achilles tendon rupture and the deep vein thrombosis with laterality and severity
Objective duplex ultrasonography or other venous imaging and any thrombophilia workup
Chronology of rupture, immobilization or treatment, and thrombosis onset
Assessment of thrombophilia, malignancy, prior venous thromboembolism, surgery, estrogen exposure, and other risk factors
Clinical assessment distinguishing injury-associated thrombosis from other etiologies

sourceReferences.citation: Nilsson-Helander K, Thurin A, Karlsson J, Eriksson BI. High incidence of deep venous thrombosis after Achilles tendon rupture: a prospective study. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2009;17(10):1234-1238. PMID 19238360. doi:10.1007/s00167-009-0727-y.
sourceReferences.note: Prospective cohort documenting a high DVT incidence after Achilles tendon rupture. It supports a bounded disease-association proposition and clinical evaluation, not automatic individual causation or aggravation.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 19238360; prospective incidence and screening discussion

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Deep vein thrombosis occurs at increased frequency after Achilles tendon rupture in cohort evidence, but population or cohort data do not establish an individual medical nexus without documentation of both conditions, compatible laterality and chronology, objective venous imaging, and competing-cause review.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation under 38 CFR § 3.310 is established by this association evidence; the mapping is not an individual nexus opinion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Lower-leg injury with immobilization can promote venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability, but the precise contribution and individual clinical pathway must be established from the patient's documented findings, venous imaging, and thrombosis-risk assessment.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Achilles tendon rupture and its immobilization are recognized injury-associated risk windows for deep vein thrombosis, but the cohort evidence does not establish that the rupture caused or aggravated DVT in every individual; both diagnoses, laterality and chronology, objective imaging, treatment, and competing thrombotic risk factors require case-specific review.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Independent rupture and DVT documentation with laterality; duplex or other venous imaging and thrombophilia workup; immobilization and chronology records; thrombophilia, malignancy, surgery, estrogen, and other competing causes; clinical assessment of the individual relationship
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Inherited or acquired thrombophilia, malignancy, or prior venous thromboembolism
Recent major surgery, hospitalization, or prolonged travel with independent immobilization
Estrogen-containing therapy, obesity, age, or other independent thrombotic risk factors
